findings.title: onlyNames bypasses real secrets via loose substring matching
findings.detail: onlyNames decides a quoted value is "just a name" (and therefore not a secret) if it matches a camelCase/dash-joined, digit-free shape AND `lower.contains(word)` for one of ["secret","token","password","passwd","key","client","vault","entry","access","name","id"]. `.contains` is a plain substring test, not a word-boundary test, and several of these words are common substrings of ordinary English words: "id" appears inside "invalid", "guide", "rapid", "wide", "side", "avoid", "decide"...; "key" appears inside "turkey", "monkey", "donkey", "hockey", "whiskey"; "entry" appears inside "sentry". A digit-free, letter-only passphrase built from ordinary words (the exact threat model the change says it still catches, e.g. "correct-horse-battery-turkey" or "invalid-wide-guide-rapid") will incidentally contain one of these substrings and be classified as onlyNames == true, so `breaks` returns false and the "password or secret" rule is silently suppressed for that line. This directly contradicts the stated guarantee ("weak passwords, passphrases and real keys still count") and reopens the exact leak this scanner exists to prevent: a plausible real secret/passphrase can now pass the secret scan and be pushed/opened in a public pull request undetected. The added test only exercises one passphrase ("correct-horse-battery-staple") that happens not to contain any of the trigger words, so the regression isn't caught by the new tests.

findings.title: onlyNames misses PascalCase/first-letter-uppercase names
findings.detail: Both wholeMatch patterns (`[a-z]+(?:[A-Z][a-z]+)+` and `[a-z]+(?:[-_.][a-z]+)+`) require the value to start with a lowercase letter. A value written PascalCase, as many non-Swift config formats use for key/value names (e.g. a .NET-style `"ClientSecret": "ClientSecret"` entry, or any value that is simply the capitalized form of the key), fails both patterns and so is treated as a real secret and still blocks the publish — one of the exact false-positive scenarios (a name for a secret, not a secret) this change is meant to fix, just for an input shape the tests don't cover.
